newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian authorities halt shipwreck salvage.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian authorities halt shipwreck salvage.

text.p: Six treasure hunters salvaging artefacts from a shipwreck off Malaysia's east coast had their passports seized by authorities who accused them of operating without a permit, the group leader said on Friday.

The six, three Swedes, two Germans and a Thai, were stopped on Tuesday as they were transferring the artefacts from their boat to a warehouse in Endau, a town in southern Johor state, Swedish engineer Sten Sjostrand told Reuters by telephone from Endau.
He said while he and his team were not in custody they had not been allowed to continue the salvage operation.

The ship, believed to be from the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644), was discovered by Sjostrand in April last year 40 nautical miles from the east coast town of Kuantan. Its cargo includes thousands of Celadon ceramic bowls and serving dishes.
Sjostrand said that Malaysian authorities including immigration officials and police accused him and his team of illegally conducting the operation.

But he said he has a letter from the Malacca museum clearing him to recover the items, and asserted he has the backing of international organisations that the area of excavation is in international waters.

"We have been taking up artefacts from international waters for the past 1-1/2 years," Sjostrand said. "We have done so under approval by various government agencies. The Endau warehouse was being guarded by local police."

Malacca chief minister Mohd Zin Abdul Ghani was quoted by the national Bernama news agency as saying on Friday that the state government has never authorised any company to salvage artefacts from any sunken vessels.
Sjostrand said there were currently 11,200 pieces of artefacts in the warehouse and that another 6,000 were being added when authorities stopped the work.
